newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Czech minister rejects fears of economic crisis.
newsitem.headline: Czech minister rejects fears of economic crisis.

text.p: The Czech economy is not in crisis and the government is able to handle some acute problems without abandoning market-oriented policies, Industry and Trade Minister Vladimir Dlouhy said on Thursday.

Speaking at an economic forum attended by French President Jacques Chirac, Dlouhy played down concern among analysts over the record 1996 trade deficit of 160.3 billion crowns ($5.6 billion), two months of falling output and budgetary pressures.
"The Czech economy is ready to face these pressures without abandoning its basic principles of liberal trade and pursuit of privatisation," he said.
"Some (analysts) say the economy is now in trouble, but 4.4 percent real GDP growth (in 1996) is not a sign of crisis. I reject all notions of a crisis in the Czech economy," he added.

Dlouhy admitted that the trade deficit, which is projected to grow to some 215 billion crowns for 1997, was a problem, but reiterated the government's position that a devaluation of the crown to spur exports was not an answer.
"I am sure that the solution of the massive (trade) deficit is not a devaluation which would only delay, and not solve the problem," he said.

After three years of a surplus, the budget dipped to a 1.56 billion crown shortfall in 1996. Parliament has passed a balanced budget for this year, though government officials say cuts will be needed soon if the goal is to be achieved.
For the first two months of 1997, the budget was in deficit by some 8.5 billion crowns. The government has blamed a slowdown in the pace of economic growth and lower tax revenues for the deficit.
On Wednesday, Dlouhy said he did not favour an import surcharge as a tool to fix the deficit.
He said would instead propose stricter adherence to existing import barriers, including enforcement of quality certification and other requirements.
